title: Timothy and Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:19–30)
hookLine: two friends honored: one who cares, one who nearly died serving

lines: AFTER THE GREAT SONG, TRAVEL PLANS.
cards: At the end of a film the credits roll: the grip, the caterer, the person who drove the van. Plenty of people are out the door before they finish.
A few lines after the great hymn of Christ emptied and lifted up, Paul's letter does something that looks almost ordinary. Travel plans. Two names.
A man who has served beside him like a son, and a man from Philippi itself who brought a gift and nearly died delivering it. The letter stops to roll the credits, and Paul reads them out slowly.

teach.b: First, Timothy. Paul is in chains, and he hopes to send Timothy to Philippi soon. In the King James Bible: "For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state."
Naturally. Not because he's told to. Timothy simply cares.

And a family picture: "as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel." Acts says Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer and his father Greek, and that Paul took him along on his travels.
Then, Epaphroditus. Everything we know about him is in this letter. The church at Philippi sent him to carry their gift to Paul in prison and to stay and help.
Somewhere along the way he fell ill.
"For indeed he was sick nigh unto death: but God had mercy on him; and not on him only, but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow."
Paul doesn't pretend. He would have grieved.
And a tender detail: Epaphroditus is homesick and heavy-hearted, not about his illness, but because the people back home heard he was ill, and he hates to think of them worrying.
So Paul sends him home: "Receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness; and hold such in reputation." Modern versions say honor.
The courier. The helper. The one who almost didn't make it back.
In a letter about Christ lowering himself, Paul shows what that looks like in two ordinary lives, and asks the church to lift them up.

how: Many churches remember helpers by name in their prayers and announcements, and some traditions honor Timothy and other companions of Paul with feast days in the church calendar.

o: Philippi's courier, who nearly died bringing their gift
the jailer in Philippi who was baptized by Paul
Paul's son in the faith who traveled with him

games.q: what's inside Philippians 2:19–30 — tap the pairs.
p: the KJV's way of saying honor

s: Epaphroditus was upset because people back home heard he was sick
he worried about their worry, so Paul sends him home.
Paul says he would not have grieved if his friend had died
he says God had mercy on him too, sparing him sorrow upon sorrow.
Timothy was one of Paul's long-time companions
Paul says he served with him in the gospel "as a son with the father."

games.q: you're Paul, in chains. your friend Epaphroditus has recovered from a near-fatal illness and is homesick. what do you do?
o: keep him with you, since you need help.
send him home, and tell the church to honor him.
games.why: Paul sends him home and asks the church to "receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness; and hold such in reputation."

practice: Think of someone who helps and is rarely thanked out loud: the person who covers the shift, the neighbor who takes in the packages, the relative who always drives.

Remember one specific thing they did, and imagine saying it by name in front of others, short and true, the way Paul did in a letter read aloud to a whole church. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Epaphroditus. The Philippians' courier who nearly died bringing their gift to Paul in prison, and whom Paul sends home asking the church to hold him in honor.

orig.note: Greek: held in honor, precious. it comes from timē, honor, the same root as the name Timothy.

carryVoice: Your line: hold such in honor. The helpers belong in the story too. Until tomorrow.
